clue.text: Deceiving daughter not easily tracked down

parts.note: something hard to find or catch is elusive

explanation.surface: A deceitful daughter who keeps slipping away from anyone trying to find her.
explanation.definitionFit: A delusive thing misleads or gives a false impression, so it is deceiving in the adjectival sense.

clue.text: Failed to work? Line taken: dismissed

indicators.note: taken here means taken away, so the letter for line is removed

parts.note: to slack is to idle, so someone who slacked failed to work

explanation.surface: An employee who skived, toed no line, and got fired for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken' means removed: SLACKED loses its L.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sacked is to be fired from a job, a common informal synonym for being let go.

clue.text: Confused boyfriend heading for town chapel, fuddled, in drink

indicators.note: in places the boyfriend, town's first letter and the jumbled chapel inside the word for drink

parts.note: ale is a drink, beer
a lover is a boyfriend

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter, here of town
fuddled means muddled or drunk, so the letters of chapel are mixed up

explanation.surface: A boyfriend in his cups, wandering drunkenly toward the town chapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fuddled' rearranges chapel, and 'heading for' takes only the T of town; the drink is split after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone all over the place is muddled and disorganised, which is to say confused.

clue.text: Drink for one before picking up summons to dine?

indicators.note: before puts the example abbreviation ahead of the rest in this down entry

parts.note: for one means for example, abbreviated eg

indicators.note: in a down clue, picking up means lifting, so the word for the summons is read upward

parts.note: a dinner gong is struck to call people to a meal

explanation.surface: A drink taken just before the dinner bell is answered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picking up' reverses GONG to GNOG in a down light.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggnog is a festive drink of eggs, milk, sugar and often spirits.

clue.text: Arts set moving into monster auditoria — occupying these?

definitions.text: Arts set moving into monster auditoria — occupying these?

indicators.note: into places the shuffled letters inside the monster plus auditoria

parts.note: an orc is a monster of fantasy fiction
auditoria are halls where audiences sit

indicators.note: moving signals that the letters of arts set are rearranged

explanation.surface: An arts crowd shifting into vast theatres, wondering where they will sit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving' rearranges the arts set letters, and they go in after the first letter of the auditoria word. The question then reads the whole clue as a picture of the people sitting there.
explanation.definitionFit: The stalls are the ground-floor seats of a theatre, the British term for the front seating in an auditorium.

clue.text: Element of weather, one interrupting American leisure and work

indicators.note: interrupting means cutting into, so the numeral for one goes inside the leisure phrase

parts.note: R and R, rest and recreation, is American slang for leisure
I is the Roman numeral one
op, short for opus, is a musical work

explanation.surface: Rain spoiling an American's time off and job alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A single drop of rain is one component or element of wet weather.

clue.text: Celebration that is involved in breaking fast

indicators.note: involved in means wrapped up inside, so the abbreviation goes within the jumbled word
breaking signals the letters of fast are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: ie, id est, is Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A party held to mark the end of a fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' rearranges fast to FSTA. Breaking a fast also means eating again, which suits a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiesta is a festival or holiday, especially in Spanish-speaking countries, so a celebration.

clue.text: Told stories about a time — recalled specific point

indicators.note: recalled is read as called back, so the whole assembly runs backwards
about means around, so the stories word surrounds the article and time

parts.note: to tell stories is to lie, so told stories means lied

explanation.surface: Someone who told tales about an incident later remembering one precise fact.
explanation.walkthrough: LIED around A and T makes LIATED; 'recalled' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: A detail is a single particular or item of information, a specific point.

clue.text: Good American sadly ignoring leader of European group

indicators.note: sadly signals that the letters are in a sorry, disordered state
ignoring leader means the first letter of the word is dropped

explanation.surface: A decent American, unhappily left out by the head of a European bloc.
explanation.walkthrough: AMERICAN loses its first letter to give MERICAN, which 'sadly' rearranges to ERMANIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Germanic describes the language family and peoples including the English, Dutch and Scandinavians, a European group.

clue.text: Screwball I then sent abroad as an invader

parts.note: a screwball is a crazy person, as is a cuckoo

indicators.note: abroad here means widely scattered, so the letters of I then sent are shuffled

explanation.surface: A crackpot confessing to sending someone overseas to invade.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes an unwelcome intruder, after the bird that lays eggs in other birds' nests.

clue.text: A source of extra heft a long time ago — before the Christian Era?

parts.note: the medieval period is a long time ago
pre is a prefix meaning before
AD, anno Domini, marks dates of the Christian Era

explanation.surface: Wondering where some extra weight came from, as if from antiquity.
explanation.walkthrough: Pre-AD would be before the Christian Era, a joke on dates that are actually AD.
explanation.definitionFit: The thickening waistline people gain around their forties and fifties is a common cause of added weight.

clue.text: Each packet's opening contributing to drink — from this?

definitions.text: Each packet's opening contributing to drink — from this?

indicators.note: contributing to means going into, so these letters are placed within the drink

parts.note: a tot is a small drink of spirits

indicators.note: a word's opening is its first letter, here of packet

explanation.surface: Every tea packet's first use goes into a brew, poured from this vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark turns the whole clue into a description: tea from the packet goes into this vessel, and the drink is poured from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot for brewing and pouring tea, which the clue presents as what the drink comes from.

clue.text: Less-than-complete balance about row in French city

indicators.note: about means around, so the shortened balance word wraps the row
less than complete means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: poise is balance or composure
a tier is a row, as of seats

explanation.surface: An incomplete bank balance causing a quarrel in a French town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less-than-complete' drops the last letter of the balance word. 'row' reads as a quarrel but means a line of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Poitiers is a historic city in west-central France, site of a famous 1356 battle.

clue.text: Escapade brought back King — prepare to move on?

indicators.note: brought back signals the escapade word is read in reverse

parts.note: a caper is an escapade or prank
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A king returned from an adventure, ready to leave again.
explanation.definitionFit: Packing things up again is what you do when getting ready to move to the next place.

clue.text: Company importing meat having nothing for French resort

indicators.note: importing means bringing in, so the company abbreviation takes the meat inside

parts.note: ham is a meat
nix is slang for nothing

explanation.surface: A firm buying in meat and receiving nothing for a French holiday spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Chamonix is a ski and mountaineering resort beneath Mont Blanc in the French Alps.

clue.text: A US lab sues us wrongly about crime — it's what you'd expect

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go around the crime
wrongly signals the letters of the fodder are arranged incorrectly

parts.note: a sin is a wrong or crime

explanation.surface: An American laboratory suing over a crime, which is only to be expected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' rearranges A US LAB SUES US around SIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means things carrying on normally, so what one would expect to happen.

clue.text: Upper-class fur ready-to-wear?

parts.note: U denotes upper-class usage
sable is a prized fur

explanation.surface: A posh fur coat, sold off the peg.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the definition stretches 'fit to use' into 'fit to wear'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something serviceable is fit for use, and clothing ready to wear is in that state.

clue.text: Quiet running water becoming piercingly loud

parts.note: sh is a call for quiet
a rill is a small stream

explanation.surface: A gentle stream turning into a deafening torrent.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrill sound is high-pitched and penetrating, so piercingly loud.

clue.text: Soft and smooth, perhaps, though containing metal

indicators.note: containing means holding inside, so the word for perhaps surrounds the metal

parts.note: say means perhaps or for example
tin is a metal

explanation.surface: Something feels soft and smooth, yet has metal in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' looks like a qualifier on the definition but is the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Satin is a glossy fabric, so something like it is soft and smooth to the touch.

clue.text: Grant, say, to import a medicine ahead of case identifying blood behaviour?

indicators.note: ahead of places the first part before the case word
import means bring in, so the actor's first name takes the article and medicine inside

parts.note: Cary Grant, the film star, is an example of a Cary
a pill is a medicine
a case at law is an action, a lawsuit

explanation.surface: An actor taking medicine before a court case about his blood.
explanation.walkthrough: Cary Grant was a Hollywood star. The question mark flags that the definition is loose: the effect also moves blood in the tiny vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: The way liquid rises in narrow tubes is linked to the finest blood vessels, hence a whimsical behaviour of blood.

clue.text: Men embraced by call reconsidered becoming a minister?

indicators.note: embraced by means held inside, so the name sits within the rearranged call
reconsidered means thought over afresh, so the letters of call are rearranged

parts.note: Eric is a man's name; the plural Men looks like a slip for Man, as the blogger also notes

explanation.surface: Men taken in by a fresh calling, which suits someone entering the ministry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reconsidered' rearranges call to CLAL. The clue prints 'Men', but only 'Man' gives a single man's name, so this is probably the setter's slip. 'becoming' means fitting, not turning into.
explanation.definitionFit: Clerical means relating to the clergy, so it describes what is fitting or proper for a churchman.

clue.text: Vegetable in church observance not entirely bad

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting observed by the church

indicators.note: not entirely means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: ill means bad, as in ill will

explanation.surface: A vegetable eaten during a church fast, which is not altogether bad.
explanation.definitionFit: A lentil is a pulse, the edible seed of a legume, loosely classed as a vegetable.
